Hi,

  This is a crosspost from js.d3 that I thought might be of interest here.

  I'm building performance analytic tools for the web at the moment, and am enjoying d3 (http://d3js.org) since I come from R where you are expected to do a similar amount of work for real graphics.

  At the moment I'm using Shiny (http://www.rstudio.com/shiny/) to supply the data, and I have hit a snag.

  Sometimes it's more convenient to supply data to d3 in wide format, either because it's the native format of the data, or it avoid processing on the server side (the client is frankly more powerful).

Note to the shiny group: My motivation here is that long format is great'n'all in R, but I don't want to transmit it across JSON because my keys are too large.  Really I need to think about relational tables but I have enough on my plate at the moment.  The scheme below is a work in progress, and doesn't include the logic to nest ID keys that I want (think county:state:town), which I've based I pretty hierarchical X axis off.  The answer to all of the below in R, is, of course, melt.  Hooray for R.

  What's wide format?  see end of message for examples, but basically it's like the result of an excel pivot; data is classified some way, such as crimes by type, and the types are arranged as columns.  What's long format? the crime type is a column, and there is a single value column for *crime count* 

  I'm struggling to import wide format elegantly into d3 from R.  There are two problems, and the second one is the harder:

First Problem

  Problem 1): R data is formatted as a list (associative map) of typed vectors (arrays).

> USArrests$name=row.names(USArrests)
> str(USArrests)
'data.frame': 50 obs. of  5 variables:
 $ Murder  : num  13.2 10 8.1 8.8 9 7.9 3.3 5.9 15.4 17.4 ...
 $ Assault : int  236 263 294 190 276 204 110 238 335 211 ...
 $ UrbanPop: int  58 48 80 50 91 78 77 72 80 60 ...
 $ Rape    : num  21.2 44.5 31 19.5 40.6 38.7 11.1 15.8 31.9 25.8 ...
 $ name    : chr  "Alabama" "Alaska" "Arizona" "Arkansas" ...

  In Javascript, this becomes:

USArrests={Murder: [13.2, 10, 8.1, 8.8],
 Assault: [236, 263, 294, 190],
 UrbanPop: [58, 48, 80, 50],
 Rape: [21.2, 44.5, 31, 19.5],
 State: ["Alabama", "Alaska", "Arizona", "Arkansas"]}

  But d3 expects an Array of Objects (associative maps).  While this doesn't seem like a hard problem, there's no builtin to d3 to do it, and I've made a mess building one.

  I need to transpose it -  this is conceptually identical to the d3.zip operator, but it takes a map (Object) as input, and an array of objects as output.

  I can muck about with keys as follows - turn it into an un-named list of arrays

USArrests_A=Object.keys(USArrests).map(function(K){return USArrests[K]})

  Transpose it

USArrests_B = d3.transpose(USArrests_A)

Here's what the first sub-array ( USArrests_B[0] ) looks like:

0: 13.2
1: 236
2: 58
3: 21.2
4: "Alabama"

  I need to re-decorate these with names:

 USArrests.C=USArrests.B.map(function(R){
   var A={};
   d3.range(0,R.length).forEach(function(i){
     A[Object.keys(USArrests)[i]]=R[i]});
     return A})

  Here's the first element, USArrests_C[0]:

Assault: 236
Murder: 13.2
Rape: 21.2
State: "Alabama"
UrbanPop: 58

Looks good! - first problem solved, although it was harder than it should be.

So now I have the Second problem

Second Problem

The next problem is that the four crimes - the measured variables (I'm going to assume Urban Pop is a musical crime) are in the same object as the state - the key or experimental variable.

Ideally I want data in the following form:

[ { State: "Alabama", Crime:"Murder", Count:13.2},
  { State: "Alabama", Crime:"Assault", Count:236}, ... ]

Although I would be satisfied with

[ { State: "Alabama", Variable:"Murder", Value:13.2},
  { State: "Alabama", Variable:"Assault", Value:236}, ... ]

This now means that each element of the array corresponds to a single visual element, such as a point, slice of a stacked bar etc.

Side note: A couple of alternative representations are:

[ { State: "Alabama", Crimes: {Murder: 13.2, Assault: 236, ... } }, { State: ... }, ... ]

and

[ { {State: "Alabama"}, {Crime: "Murder"}, 13.2 },
{ {State: "Alabama"}, {Crime: "Murder"}, 13.2 }, ... ] 

Which might seem odd, but it allows the keys to be compound or have metadata, which is shared between all crimes in Alabama:

[ { {State: "Alabama", Country: "US"}, {Crime: "Murder", Color: "Red"}, 13.2 },  

However, the first representation is not friendly to d3, and the second is good but outside the scope of my question.

So how do I get here:

[ { State: "Alabama", Variable:"Murder", Value:13.2},
  { State: "Alabama", Variable:"Assault", Value:236}, ... ]

The first problem is that in the original data, the experimental variables (state) are conflated with the response variables, and we need some extra information to extract them.

One approach (taken by R's reshape2 package) is to treat enumerations and strings as experimental and numbers are response variables, which would work in this case, but I'm going to ignore that and just supply the extra missing information.  This seems like an OK strategy to me because I'm going to have to map variables to x and y (and color etc) at some point, and the same basic information is required for that too.

> idKeys = ["State"]
> valueKeys = Object.keys(USArrests).filter(function(x){return x!= idKeys})
["Murder", "Assault", "UrbanPop", "Rape"]

Excellent - but how do I use this information?

Here's where I start to get into trouble, and the fact that I'me been programming javascript for all of 20 hours starts to show.

USArrests_D = USArrests_C.map(function(I){
  return valueKeys.map(function(VK){
    N={};                                         // a new object for each Value Key
    idKeys.forEach(function(IDK){N[IDK]=I[IDK]}); // copy the ID Keys in
    N[VK]=R[VK]; return N;})})                    // and the Value Key

That produces a nested list, which needs flattening:

USArrests_E=[].concat.apply([],USArrests_D)

Which produces the following array:

[{Murder: 13.2, State: "Alabama"},{Assault: 236,State: "Alabama"},... ]

Which is what we want - d3 can nicely process this using the data() function.

The Question:

Is there a better way?  Can d3 add a map zip? What bits of my code could you do shorter, or neater, or with less bugs?  Is this even a problem for anyone else.

I mostly program in R, so please excuse ( but point out ) the inadequacy of my js code.


Appendix: Examples of Wide and Long format:

  Wide format:

> head(n=4,USArrests)

I'm not 100% sure this is what you're looking for, but you can use
split() to turn it into a list of data frames, where there is one list
element for each row of the original data frame. Each of these list
elements is a one-row data frame with the same original columns.

For example:
> x <- split(USArrests, seq_len(nrow(USArrests)))
> head(x, 3)
$`1`

Murder Assault UrbanPop Rape
Alabama 13.2 236 58 21.2

$`2`
Murder Assault UrbanPop Rape
Alaska 10 263 48 44.5

$`3`
Murder Assault UrbanPop Rape
Arizona 8.1 294 80 31


> str(x)
List of 50
$ 1 :'data.frame': 1 obs. of 4 variables:
..$ Murder : num 13.2
..$ Assault : int 236
..$ UrbanPop: int 58
..$ Rape : num 21.2
$ 2 :'data.frame': 1 obs. of 4 variables:
..$ Murder : num 10
..$ Assault : int 263
..$ UrbanPop: int 48
..$ Rape : num 44.5
$ 3 :'data.frame': 1 obs. of 4 variables:
..$ Murder : num 8.1
..$ Assault : int 294
..$ UrbanPop: int 80
..$ Rape : num 31


The elements are named "1", "2", and so on, but you can remove the
names with unname(x).

-Winston
